title: Run work on an executor
summary: Split a count across two tasks, collect the futures, and shut the pool down.

scenario.briefing: A large inventory scan blocks the request thread. Split the scan across two pool tasks, combine the futures, and make sure the executor is always shut down.

objectives.description: Submit the scan work to an executor and collect results.
Diagnose a pool that is never shut down.
Explain futures, shutdown, and shared state accurately.

hints: Create one fixed pool for the two halves.
submit accepts a Callable and returns a Future.
Collect both results with get before returning.
Shut the executor down in a finally block.

misconceptions.description: Leaving the scan on the request thread.
misconceptions.testDescription: The work is submitted to an executor.
misconceptions.feedback: The point is to move the work off the caller. Submit the two halves and combine their futures.

misconceptions.description: Relying on garbage collection to stop a pool.
misconceptions.feedback: Garbage collection does not shut down worker threads deterministically. Call shutdown in a finally block.

misconceptions.description: Believing Future.get starts the task again.
misconceptions.feedback: The task starts when it is submitted. get waits for the existing result and propagates failure.

sections.title: Executors manage threads
sections.body: An ExecutorService owns a pool of worker threads and accepts tasks. submit returns a Future that represents the pending result. get waits for completion and propagates exceptions wrapped in ExecutionException. Reusing a pool avoids the cost of creating a thread per request.

sections.title: Shut down the pool
sections.body: shutdown stops accepting new tasks and lets submitted tasks finish. shutdownNow attempts to interrupt running tasks. A pool that is never shut down can keep a JVM alive and leak threads in a long-running test suite.

sections.title: Shared mutable state needs coordination
sections.body: Two tasks that write the same variable without synchronization create a data race. Use task-local results, synchronization, or atomic classes such as AtomicInteger. Prefer returning values from tasks over mutating shared state.
